pages.x: A century after Caesar's raids, the emperor Claudius, who needed a victory, sent four legions across the Channel in AD 43. They beat the Britons under Caratacus and his brother on the river Medway in a two-day battle and crossed the Thames.

Claudius came over himself, for just 16 days, bringing elephants, to lead his army into Camulodunum, now Colchester, the chief town of the strongest British tribe. On his arch in Rome an inscription boasted that eleven British kings had surrendered to him.

Caratacus fought on in the hills of Wales for eight years, until Cartimandua, queen of the Brigantes, handed him over in chains. Brought to Rome, he spoke so proudly before Claudius, Tacitus says, that the emperor spared him and his family.

In 60 the governor, Suetonius Paulinus, attacked Mona, now Anglesey, the stronghold of the druids. Tacitus describes women in black with torches running among the warriors, and druids raising their hands to the sky with curses, until the legionaries steadied and cut them down.

Meanwhile the Iceni rose. Their king had left half his kingdom to the emperor, but Roman officials seized it all, flogged his widow Boudica and raped her daughters. She led the Iceni and their neighbours to burn Camulodunum, London and Verulamium. Tacitus says 70,000 people died.

Suetonius faced her vast army with about 10,000 men, in a narrow valley with woods behind him. The tight Roman ranks broke the charge, and the Britons were trapped against their own wagons. Boudica died soon after, of poison, Tacitus says.

The legions pushed on into Wales and Scotland. In 83 or 84 the governor Agricola beat the Caledonians at Mons Graupius, somewhere in the Highlands. Tacitus, his son-in-law, gave their leader a famous line about Rome: they make a desert and call it peace.
Rome never held the far north. In 122 the emperor Hadrian ordered a wall of stone and turf 117 km long, coast to coast, with a small fort every Roman mile.
pages.fx: It marked the empire's edge for nearly 300 years, and long stretches still stand. Letters on wooden tablets from a fort nearby tell of soldiers' daily lives.

pages.x: Britain was Roman for nearly 400 years, until about 410. The Romans founded London, built roads that modern ones still follow, and brought towns, baths and Latin. Boudica, who almost drove them out, became a heroine, and her statue stands by the Houses of Parliament.
